title: Chasing Liberty
full_review:
Teenage dating has never been easy. But when your father happens to be the leader of the free world the normally awkward enterprise can be downright impossible. This dating dilemma forms the framework of Andy Cadiff's "Chasing Liberty" (Warner Bros.), a flavorless romantic comedy about a president's daughter who goes AWOL while accompanying her parents on a state visit to Europe.

Pop singer Mandy Moore stars as 18-year-old Anna Foster (Secret Service designation "Liberty"), a frustrated first daughter fed up with her every move being monitored by a vanload of bodyguards -- men-in-black government chaperones have a way of cramping one's social life. Despite having lived her whole life in the public eye, she is just a normal angst-ridden adolescent -- a fragile melange of defiance and insecurity.

Mark Harmon plays her two-term presidential father, who, while holding a 63 percent approval rating, is in the dark about, er, domestic policies. Like most overprotective dads he is reluctant to admit his little girl has grown up -- yet unlike most he must juggle paternal panic with the economic fate of developing Third World nations.

While attending a G8 conference in Prague with the first folks, Anna shows off some diplomacy of her own by striking a bargain with her father which will allow her one night out on the town as a "normal" teenager, unencumbered by a phalanx of Secret Service agents. But when he reneges and actually beefs up her pared-down security detail, Anna gives her handlers the slip at a local club, and, aided and abetted by a dashing young Brit named Ben Calder (Matthew Goode), embarks on an impromptu barnstorming tour of Europe.

However, unbeknownst to Anna, Ben is actually a CIA field agent planted by her dad to keep an eye on her while she enjoys the illusion of independence. Needless to say, his undercover assignment ends up under the covers, making his inevitable coming clean about the deception all the more devastating to Anna.
Having grown up in the spotlight, Moore is well-groomed for the role, though the subplot involving her romantically gun-shy handlers (played by Jeremy Piven and Annabella Sciorra) proves far more entertaining than her pouting and pining. Apart from a mildly amusing opening sequence at 1600 Pennsylvania Ave. which puts a cute spin on pre-date jitters, much of the humor is flat and caters to ethnic stereotyping.

On its surface the film is a breezy story about a girl at a crossroads in her life. Stripped of the commander-in-chief complications, Anna's dilemma is no different than that of any teen struggling with independence and identity issues. Likewise, while few if any parents have access to stealth helicopters to track their son or daughter's whereabouts, her father's sheltering instinct resonates with any parent who finds it difficult to cut the proverbial apron strings.

However, if the filmmaker's intent is to argue for parents trusting their children, he presents a rather self-incriminating case. From the outset, Anna proves that she is anything but responsible, getting drunk, stripping for a quick skinny-dip in the Danube and, after one magical kiss on a romantic gondola ride in Venice, deciding that she is ready to sleep with Ben, a guy she barely knows.

Underneath its fresh-scrubbed facade, the film seems more concerned with the pursuit of happiness than life or liberty. And the "happiness" sought is not what St. Thomas Aquinas would call the "summa bonum" (the final good) but a cheap hedonism, exemplified by "The Love Parade," an orgiastic Mardi Gras-like rave at which Anna and Ben wind up in Berlin. During the bacchanalia a song proclaims, "You've got to live your life free to do what you want to do," exposing the film's underlying message of false emancipation. What is being chased is not liberty, but libertinism. Moore's 1999 debut album, "So Real," struck gold with the hit single "Candy," which is exactly what this movie is -- sugary sweet, but ultimately corrosive.

Due to an implied sexual encounter, some sexual humor, brief rear nudity, and minimal mildly crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
